messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 53
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Bus Driver
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 76

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Feeling Tired: Feeling very tired or exhausted, Driving with Others: Driving with people, Auditory (Sounds): Related sounds
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
  Negative Appraisals: Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# James

James was fifty-three when he came to his first therapy appointment, and he had not slept more than four hours in a single night for nearly two years. His wife, Carmen, had insisted he make the call. She sat beside him in the waiting room, her hand resting on his knee, a gesture he had come to associate less with comfort and more with the weight of her worry—a worry he felt responsible for, which only made the exhaustion worse.

The event itself had occurred on a Tuesday evening in October, just after nine o'clock. James had been working the late route for the municipal transit authority, a job he had held for twenty-eight years. A passenger had boarded near downtown, an older man in dark clothes whom James had not paid particular attention to initially. The bus had emptied out gradually as the evening deepened, and by the time they reached the industrial section near the yards, there was no one left but the two of them. The man had moved toward James, and what followed was a violent assault that James still could not speak about in complete sentences. He had been forced, overpowered, and left bleeding in the driver's seat while the man fled into the darkness.

The police had come. The hospital had come. The investigation had gone nowhere.

What had come, relentlessly, was the memory itself—not as a distant recollection but as something that erupted without warning, frame by frame, with the same suffocating terror he had felt in that moment. The sensation of being trapped in the driver's seat, the weight of the man's body, the sounds of struggle and breathing—these would return to him with photographic clarity, often triggered by the most mundane circumstances. When he felt exhausted, his guard seemed to lower, and the memories would flood in. Driving with other people in the vehicle became intolerable; the presence of a passenger—any passenger—made his skin crawl, made him feel exposed and vulnerable in a way that felt shameful even to acknowledge. Certain sounds, too: the hydraulic hiss of bus doors, a particular cadence of footsteps behind him, even the radio playing at certain volumes could transport him back to that night with startling immediacy.

What frightened James most was not just the memory itself but what the memory meant about the world and about himself. He had come to believe that people could not be trusted—not really, not underneath whatever courtesy or normalcy they displayed. He had worked with the public for nearly three decades and had thought of himself as someone who understood human nature. That faith had shattered. He found himself scrutinizing every passenger who boarded, cataloging exits, sitting in positions that allowed him to see both mirrors and the cabin behind him. The company had eventually moved him to administrative duties after several incidents where he had become aggressive with passengers, but even that felt like a failure, another way the assault had stolen something from him.

Worse than the loss of faith in others was the shame that clung to his own body. When Carmen reached for him in the darkness, he would tense and pull away, unable to explain why his own skin felt like a crime scene, why he could not tolerate being touched in certain ways without feeling that he was somehow complicit in what had happened to him. He had stopped going to church, where he had worshiped for forty years, because he could not reconcile his faith with what had been done to him, and because he was no longer certain that God saw him as anything but damaged. The exhaustion fed everything—when he was tired, his defenses crumbled, and the memories came with full sensory force. He had begun sleeping in the spare room, telling Carmen it was so his thrashing would not disturb her, but they both knew it was something else entirely.

It was Carmen, finally, who had broken the silence. She had found him one morning sitting on the back porch at five in the morning, shaking, and she had simply said that he could not continue like this, that whatever had happened to him in that bus, it was happening to both of them now, and they needed help. James had resisted for weeks, but the weight of her sadness had finally pushed him toward the phone. He sat in the therapy office now, exhausted and ashamed, hoping that someone could help him understand why he had come to believe that he was no longer safe in his own body, and whether it was possible to drive again without feeling like prey.
